patients.label: Case 1: 50-year-old man with next-day recurrent chest pain and acute cholangitis

identity_evidence.quote: A 50-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a sudden onset of intermittent, stinging chest pain lasting for two hours. By the time he arrived at the hospital, the pain had subsided, and his vital signs were stable. A 12-lead electrocardiography (ECG) revealed a left bundle branch block, which was also present on a previous ECG (Figure 1). The Sgarbossa criteria were considered but not met []. Cardiac biomarkers were within normal limits, whereas liver enzymes were mildly elevated (Table 1). Because the chest pain had resolved and ACS was deemed unlikely, the patient was discharged.

A 50-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a sudden onset of intermittent, stinging chest pain lasting for two hours. By the time he arrived at the hospital, the pain had subsided, and his vital signs were stable. A 12-lead electrocardiography (ECG) revealed a left bundle branch block, which was also present on a previous ECG (Figure 1). The Sgarbossa criteria were considered but not met []. Cardiac biomarkers were within normal limits, whereas liver enzymes were mildly elevated (Table 1). Because the chest pain had resolved and ACS was deemed unlikely, the patient was discharged.

The following day, he experienced recurrent chest pain and was transported via emergency medical services to the Tokyo Coronary Care Unit (CCU) Network with suspected ACS. He complained of chest pain and nausea. On arrival, the patient was alert (Glasgow Coma Scale E4V5M6). His vital signs were stable: respiratory rate, 18 breaths per minute; pulse, 72 beats per minute; blood pressure, 139/85 mmHg; oxygen saturation, 97% on room air; and body temperature, 36.8°C. Pupils were equal at 3 mm bilaterally and reactive to light.

Physical examination revealed no conjunctival pallor or scleral icterus. Breath sounds were clear bilaterally, and no cardiac murmurs were heard. He reported spontaneous pain extending from the anterior chest to the epigastric region, but there was no tenderness on palpation. The abdomen was flat and soft, with normal bowel sounds, and no lower extremity edema was observed. The ECG findings were unchanged from the previous day. Cardiac markers remained within normal limits; however, liver enzymes had worsened (Table 1). A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan was performed to evaluate the liver function abnormalities, revealing dilation of the common bile duct and the presence of common bile duct stones (Figure 2).

According to the Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18) diagnostic criteria, the presence of systemic inflammation (mild leukocytosis), cholestasis (elevated biliary enzymes), and imaging findings of choledocholithiasis fulfilled the diagnosis of mild acute cholangitis. Guideline-directed intravenous cefmetazole therapy was initiated the same day, and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) was performed electively on day 2. Bile culture grew Peptoniphilus asaccharolyticus, which was susceptible to cefmetazole. Antibiotic therapy was continued for seven days, and the patient was discharged without symptoms on day 8.

summary.text: Case 1 was a 50-year-old man with no significant medical history and two hours of sudden intermittent stinging chest pain, resolved before first arrival. ECG showed preexisting LBBB and did not meet Sgarbossa criteria. Normal cardiac biomarkers and mildly elevated liver enzymes led to discharge, return instructions and arranged follow-up; abdominal imaging was not performed.

The next day recurrent chest pain and nausea prompted EMS/CCU-network transport for suspected ACS. Vitals and cardiac markers remained stable/normal, ECG was unchanged and liver enzymes worsened. CT showed CBD dilation/stones, establishing mild acute cholangitis by TG18. IV cefmetazole began the same day; elective ERCP occurred on day 2. summary.text: Case 2, a 50-year-old man one month after STEMI and PCI, developed sudden epigastric pain resembling his earlier cardiac event and anterior chest-to-epigastric pain. He was transported via the Tokyo CCU Network for possible recurrent ACS. Cardiac markers were normal; ECG showed T-wave inversion in I/aVL without ST elevation, while leukocytosis and mildly elevated biliary enzymes/amylase were present.

CT showed enlarged thick-walled gallbladder and repeat examination a positive Murphy’s sign, making acute cholecystitis most likely by TG18. Ultrasound and local serial troponins were not performed, a baseline ECG was unavailable, and stent-related complications were not completely excluded. He was transferred to the prior PCI hospital for biliary management and cardiac reevaluation, where laparoscopic cholecystectomy confirmed cholecystitis. Discussion documents IV antibiotics and symptom resolution without naming the Case 2 antibiotic or giving discharge timing.

events.description: Clinic referral for suspected angina and initial ED presentation/workup

evidence.quote: A 77-year-old man with a history of hypertension and dyslipidemia presented with anterior chest and epigastric pain at rest. He was referred to our ED from a local clinic because of suspected angina. On arrival, the patient reported pain extending from the left anterior chest to the epigastrium. The patient was alert (Glasgow Coma Scale E4V5M6). His vital signs were as follows: respiratory rate, 16 breaths per minute; pulse, 79 beats per minute; blood pressure, 149/85 mmHg; oxygen saturation, 96% on room air; and body temperature, 36.9℃. Pupils were equal at 3 mm bilaterally and reactive to light. Physical examination revealed no conjunctival pallor, scleral icterus, or cervical lymphadenopathy. Breath sounds were clear bilaterally, and no cardiac murmurs were heard. The patient reported spontaneous pain extending from the anterior chest to the epigastric region, with tenderness on palpation. The abdomen was soft and flat, with normal bowel sounds, and no lower extremity edema was noted. ECG showed no significant abnormalities (Figure 5), and cardiac markers remained within normal limits; however, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and γ-GTP were slightly elevated. White C-reactive protein (CRP) was elevated (Table 3).

events.description: Repeat Murphy sign and TG18 supported cholecystitis; risk/fitness assessment

evidence.quote: Although serial measurements and cardiology consultation were not performed, the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) risk score was calculated as 2 (age ≥65 years and two coronary risk factors: hypertension and dyslipidemia), indicating intermediate risk. A repeat physical examination confirmed a positive Murphy’s sign. According to the TG18 diagnostic criteria, the patient fulfilled the requirements for acute cholecystitis, showing local signs (positive Murphy’s sign), systemic inflammation, and imaging findings. Although the TIMI risk score was 2, indicating an intermediate risk, acute cholecystitis was considered the most likely cause of the chest pain. With a Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) of 4 and an American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status (ASA-PS) of 2, the patient was deemed fit for surgery, and a laparoscopic cholecystectomy was performed on the same day. Intravenous cefmetazole (CMZ) was administered from the day of admission until hospital day 4, and the patient was discharged ambulatory on day 5.

summary.text: Case 3, a 77-year-old man with hypertension and dyslipidemia, was referred for suspected angina after left anterior chest-to-epigastric pain at rest. Examination found palpation tenderness with otherwise documented normal/negative cardiopulmonary and abdominal findings. ECG and cardiac markers were normal; biliary enzymes and inflammatory markers were elevated.

Contrast CT showed gallstones and an enlarged thick-walled gallbladder. Repeat Murphy’s sign was positive and TG18 supported acute cholecystitis as the most likely pain cause. Ultrasound, serial cardiac measurements and cardiology consultation were not performed. TIMI was 2 with author interpretation of intermediate risk; CCI 4 and ASA-PS 2 supported surgical fitness. Same-day laparoscopic cholecystectomy and IV cefmetazole through day 4 were followed by symptom resolution and ambulatory discharge on day 5.
